posts.note: Long ADHD explainer addressed to a family member. Mostly present-tense clinical claims and study reviews; forward-looking items are pipeline-treatment calls, Monarch eTNS adoption claims, a never-call about causal evidence, and repeated prognoses for one child. Contains recycled text ('For me, in 2023').

Capability checklist payers want for value-based behavioral health contracts; the list itself is payer requirements, not author forecasts. Three general claims about contract timing and conversion logged.
Draft memoir chapter about a childhood tornado; narrative dialogue only. One own-project claim about the book.
Satirical song lyrics in an imagined Vivek Ramaswamy voice about DOGE; no sincere forecast in the lyrics. One newsletter programming plan logged.
Re-shared narrative medicine piece about a Cotard delusion patient; no forward-looking statements by the author.

statements.quote: Your kid is most likely to do great .
statements.context: Opening advice to a family member whose child has ADHD. The author asserts ADHD is one of the most treatable conditions in psychiatry and predicts the child's long-term outcome.
statements.note: Clinical prognosis for one child, not a market or regulatory call; restated twice near the end of the post.

statements.quote: There is absolutely more effective treatment coming. There are treatments in the pipeline that are not here right now, like low-dose LSD for ADHD, probably TMS for ADHD, maybe even transcranial focused ultrasound, we may get fMRI-EEG neurofeedback, I don't actually know. I do know there's likely to be more in the future.
statements.context: After listing current ADHD treatments (stimulants, organizational skills training, the Monarch eTNS device), the author forecasts that more effective ADHD treatments will arrive and names pipeline candidates.
statements.confidence_phrase: absolutely; probably; maybe even; may; likely
statements.note: Compound claim: one general call plus four hedged candidate treatments, each with its own confidence word.

statements.quote: as your kid gets older, their brain is going to develop, and they're going to grow out of a lot of these symptoms
statements.context: Argument that even if stimulants were the only treatment, brain development will reduce the child's ADHD symptoms over time.
statements.note: General developmental claim applied to one child; borderline truism about ADHD natural history.

statements.quote: So we're never gonna have the rock-solid causality answer, we're only gonna strongly suspect that the treatment that reduces symptoms is good in a long-term.
statements.context: The author says long-term randomized trials that withhold ADHD treatment from children would be unethical, so causal proof that childhood treatment reduces adult ADHD burden will never exist.
statements.note: Negative call about future evidence in general, not about a named trial.

statements.quote: I am highly skeptical any of those therapists are who you will match with on Talkspace.
statements.context: Discussion of organizational skills training (OST), the one psychotherapy the author says works for ADHD executive dysfunction; he doubts a Talkspace user will be matched with an OST-trained therapist.
statements.note: Borderline: a claim about Talkspace's current therapist pool phrased as what a future user will get.

statements.quote: The next generation of treatments are exciting. They promise better efficacy and a lower side effect profile.
statements.context: After listing novel ADHD treatments under research (TMS, the FDA-approved Monarch eTNS device, and LSD derivatives in clinical trials sponsored by Mind Medicine), the author expects the next generation to beat current treatments on efficacy and side effects.
statements.note: Expectation about a class of treatments; no single trial readout named.

statements.quote: a long-acting form of clonidine, a frequently used alpha 2 agonist, is in the process of being developed for use in ADHD.
statements.context: Closing sentence of a block quote from a 2013 review of alpha agonists (clonidine, guanfacine, Intuniv) in ADHD. The author then writes 'For me, in 2023, the above still holds', adopting the review's statements.
statements.confidence_phrase: is in the process of being developed
statements.note: Third-party text (2013 review) endorsed by the author; the endorsement says 'in 2023' though the post is dated 2025, so recycled text.

statements.quote: We need more evidence and novel treatments, and as you can see above, they're coming
statements.context: The author's endorsement right after the 2013 alpha-agonist review quote; he asserts that novel ADHD treatments are on the way.
statements.note: Restatement of the earlier 'more effective treatment coming' call; the sentence begins 'For me, in 2023', so recycled text.

statements.quote: But, it’s more likely your ADHD will kill your kid earlier on its own if left untreated.
statements.context: Summary of the cardiovascular-risk section. The author accepts that ADHD medication may raise cardiovascular risk over many years but expects untreated ADHD to cause earlier death, citing Swedish registry mortality data.
statements.note: Risk comparison from published cohort studies, framed as a prognosis for the reader's child; borderline.

statements.quote: Cause they have a problem that leads to early death—at 68, not 76—if people don’t take care of themselves. But those causes of early death are all preventable.
statements.context: Advice section after a BMJ life-expectancy study showing 7 to 9 fewer years for adults with ADHD. The author restates the gap as a conditional prognosis and asserts the causes (smoking, alcohol, suicide) are preventable.
statements.note: Conditional restatement of epidemiological data with a numeric age gap; borderline forecast.

statements.quote: I try mine tonight.
statements.context: Description of the Monarch eTNS device, which is worn during sleep; the author says he will try his own device that night.
statements.note: Personal plan with no forecast value; coder may mark CONTROL or drop.

statements.quote: It is a revolution in ADHD for kids and another example of the Neuro-modulated future of our field.
statements.context: The author argues the Monarch eTNS device should be first-line for pediatric ADHD and frames it as evidence that psychiatry's future is neuromodulation.
statements.note: Directional claim about the field. The author's practice Fermata offers the device, a conflict he flags in the post.

statements.quote: If physicians prescribe this medical device, which is not a controlled substance, they may avoid stimulants in many cases.
statements.context: Efficacy section on the Monarch eTNS device; conditional claim that prescribing it would let physicians avoid stimulant medication for many children.
statements.note: Conditional practice claim.

statements.quote: I don't think we solve ADHD at scale by doing things that aren't scalable.
statements.context: Closing argument that the ADHD treatment crisis (stimulant shortages, DEA constraints, prescribing hassle) is solved by better treatments such as Monarch eTNS rather than by more stimulant prescribing; the author cites a hard limit on stimulant supply.
statements.note: Negative call about how the treatment crisis resolves; borderline general claim.

statements.quote: Your kids gonna be OK. That's the most likely outcome.
statements.context: 'Wrapping It All Up' section; prognosis for the family member's child, backed by the author's tens of thousands of clinical hours.
statements.note: Restatement of the opening prognosis.

statements.quote: It's gonna be OK if they have to take a stimulant. That stimulant is probably gonna work.
statements.context: Same closing section; the author predicts stimulant treatment will work for the child, allowing for dose, formulation, or combination adjustments.
statements.note: Prognosis for one child's medication response; the passage goes on to list possible adjustments before 'it's gonna be really helpful'.

statements.quote: Your kid's gonna be OK, the treatment is highly likely to help, and if you stick with it, you're gonna be really happy that you did so.
statements.context: Final sentence of advice; restated prognosis with a conditional on sticking with treatment.
statements.note: Third restatement of the prognosis.

statements.quote: Much like bonsai trees, value based contracts take years of careful pruning.
statements.context: Photo caption in a post on how to reach a value-based behavioral health contract with a major payer, drawn from the author's 18 months of negotiations with UnitedHealth Group leadership; he asserts such contracts take years.
statements.note: General timing claim from experience, not a dated forecast; borderline.

statements.quote: I'm not saying it's going to get you a contract, even if you have it all.
statements.context: After listing the capabilities Big Health payers say they want for value-based mental health contracts, the author warns that having every capability does not guarantee a contract.
statements.confidence_phrase: I'm not saying it's going to
statements.note: Hedged negative caveat about contract outcomes rather than a positive call.

statements.quote: The best predictor of a pilot turning into a contract and subsequently, a major program is the stability of leadership in the company.
statements.context: Footnote warning that what payer insiders say they want and what they can sign differ; leadership changes killed pilots at the author's companies, so he names leadership stability as the predictor of a pilot becoming a contract.
statements.note: General predictive heuristic, not a dated call; borderline.

statements.quote: The book is non-fiction and an autobiography. Buckle up people. It's gonna be exciting. In theory.
statements.context: Intro to a draft memoir chapter; the author says he is writing a book and predicts it will be exciting.
statements.note: Own-project claim about a book in progress, self-hedged with 'In theory'; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I was working on an article before I did this about a research study, and I'm gonna get back to that.
statements.context: Opening of a satirical song post about Vivek Ramaswamy watching DOGE from the sidelines; the author promises to return to an article about a research study.
statements.note: Newsletter programming plan; the song lyrics are satire in an imagined voice and carry no sincere forecast.
